title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
description: At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turke
body: At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17.Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

schema.headline: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people

title: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut
description: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New Yo
body: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year. However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn. Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

schema.headline: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut

title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo
description: A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a sho
body: A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit."While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added. The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said. A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion. A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect. Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion. "Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.Spanish opposition leader and President of the People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "What happened in Oviedo is heartbreaking."My condolences to the family of the officer who died and my best wishes for the recovery of the one who was seriously injured.

schema.headline: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo

title: Tyler Robinson: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk shooter set for June 2028
description: The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.Robinson, 23,
body: The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated  a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs."There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September."We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

schema.headline: Tyler Robinson: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk shooter set for June 2028

title: First day of Ukraine peace talks 'very productive', US says
description: The first day of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi. While senior offic
body: The first day of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi. While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions - due to resume on Wednesday - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who did not attend the talks, said they had been "very productive".Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".Kushner said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting. European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks until now, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them. The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture"."They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.From the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine that "might involve all of Europe".Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result in a fair peace. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.The only way to make Russia's Vladimir Putin start real negotiations was by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said."While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi includes Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.Kyiv has sent several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof that Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations"."This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

schema.headline: First day of Ukraine peace talks 'very productive', US says

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
description: Figure caption, The BBC's Ione Wells on how the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apartByNardine SaadA Massachusetts judge ha
body: Figure caption, The BBC's Ione Wells on how the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apartByNardine SaadA Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against  Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative. The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight. Image source, Getty ImagesIn his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said."Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath. He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's  defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict. The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant. Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case

title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
description: Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.Moataz Daghlas wa
body: Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.

schema.headline: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says

title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
description: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI ha
body: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology"."The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said. One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told. Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

schema.headline: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack

title: Nagaland: Oxford museum returns ancestral  Naga skulls to India
description: The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were
body: The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains. These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.The museum's website, external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains."The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP."I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

schema.headline: Nagaland: Oxford museum returns ancestral  Naga skulls to India

title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
description: Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is
body: Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared. Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.Both are innovators revered in the tech world.  However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models. In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200. An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case."President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders. However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles. Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement. The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern". He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".What does this show us? At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views. More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy. Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health. It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security

title: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home
description: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the
body: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home."My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models."My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women. Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, externalAn email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier. "Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims."Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineLawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves."These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times."People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".Roza says at the moment, "there's no justice for me, nothing's going to make everything go away".But she hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward."There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

schema.headline: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home

title: Krakow attack: Polish unity on show as thousands join silent march for shooting victims
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attackBySar
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attackBySarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromKrakowThousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower. Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died.Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology."The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised."So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."There has been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.It is alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone diedTwo days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.Image caption, Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasionOlha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she said."It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on MondayWhen Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass."This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life.""Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish."People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without being held to account for the devastation."I think we deserve to know why."

schema.headline: Krakow attack: Polish unity on show as thousands join silent march for shooting victims

title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
description: Figure caption, Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBCByJames WaterhouseParis correspo
body: Figure caption, Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBCByJames WaterhouseParis correspondentWarning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violenceAlthough she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022."We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.Image source, Social mediaImage caption, A still image from one of DZ Mafia's notorious video statementsThe city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.Inside Marseille's drug gangs - watch on YouTube now, externalFrance's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Karine was called by a doctor about her son Hugo: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head"Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille."He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.That area was Quartier Nord.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, DZ Mafia wields power in Marseille's Quartier NordOur best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road."I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave."Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Camil, who claims to have left DZ Mafia, only agreed to speak to the BBC away from the city - on a boatMoney is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members."They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains."You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders."People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking"."Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy,  slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."Image source, Marianne Baisnee / BBCImage caption, "Thank you, see you soon" reads graffiti on a wall, alongside price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuanaWe challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets."If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.Image source, Lea Guedj / BBCImage caption, Gang member "Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) per month aged 13We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here."Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause."It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy"."We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."Image source, Social mediaImage caption, DZ Mafia members filmed firing guns from a balcony in Marseille - the footage was then posted on social mediaPolice have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life."These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo. The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnee, Lea Guedj and Paul Pradier

schema.headline: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill

title: Villa Vie Odyssey: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
description: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore. The Odys
body: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore. The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said."Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website. "For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

schema.headline: Villa Vie Odyssey: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore

title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
description: Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The former arm
body: Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months. One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government. Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside. If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs. In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc. Netanyahu - Israel's longest-serving leader - reiterated in a video on Monday his call for the formation of a government of national unity, which he said he would lead as prime minister.He said any Zionist party - those which support Israel as a Jewish state - including opposition parties, would be eligible. He warned against a government which relied on what he called "the Islamists", an apparent reference to Arab parties."You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he said.

schema.headline: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
